title: Mastering Diabetic Macular Edema (DME)
summary: Diabetic Macular Edema (DME) is the leading cause of moderate vision loss in the working-age population. This poster provides a deep-dive into its pathophysiology, evidence-based management, and the latest landmark clinical trials.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: DME is defined as retinal thickening or hard exudate accumulation within 1 disc diameter of the center of the macula. It results from the breakdown of the inner Blood-Retinal Barrier (BRB), leading to the leakage of fluid and plasma constituents into the intraretinal layers, specifically the Outer Plexiform Layer (Henle's layer) and Inner Nuclear Layer.

branches: VEGF Pathway: Upregulation due to hypoxia
Angiopoietin-2: Competes with Ang-1 for Tie2 receptor
Leukostasis: Neutrophil adhesion to capillary endothelium
Oxidative Stress: PKC pathway & Polyol pathway activation
Pericyte Loss: Leading to microaneurysm formation

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Microaneurysms (MAs): Earliest sign, focal leakage points.
Hard Exudates (HE): Lipid deposits, often in circinate patterns.
Retinal Edema: Thickening/clouding of the macula.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Fluid pockets in a petaloid pattern.
Ischemic Maculopathy: Enlarged Foveal Avascular Zone (FAZ).
Vitreomacular Interface issues: Epiretinal membranes (ERM).

rows: Hard Exudates within 500µm of center + thickening
Thickening ≥ 1 disc area within 1 DD of center

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: BCVA & Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (90D lens) for baseline.
Step 2: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) to measure CST and identify IRF/SRF.
Step 3: Fluorescein Angiography (FA) to differentiate Focal vs. Diffuse leakage.
Step 4: OCT-Angiography (OCT-A) to assess FAZ and capillary non-perfusion.
Step 5: Fundus Photography for longitudinal tracking of hard exudates.

rows: Post-cataract surgery, classic petaloid leakage on FA.
Widespread flame hemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins.
White dots, vitreous cells, younger demographic.
Visible VMT or ERM on OCT causing mechanical pull.

sections.title: Medical Management: The Systemic 'Big Three'
content: Glycemic Control: Target HbA1c < 7.0% (DCCT/UKPDS).
Blood Pressure Control: Target < 130/80 mmHg.
Lipid Management: Statins to reduce hard exudate accumulation (FIELD study).
Renal Function: Monitoring GFR and albuminuria.

rows: 2mg (VIVID/VISTA) - VEGF Trap, binds VEGF-A, B, PlGF

sections.title: Corticosteroid Implants
content: Ozurdex (Dexamethasone 0.7mg): 3-6 month duration, biodegradable.
Iluvien (Fluocinolone 0.19mg): 36 month duration, non-biodegradable.
Indications: Chronic DME, pseudophakic patients, anti-VEGF non-responders.
Side Effects: Cataract progression (near 100%), IOP elevation (approx 30%).

sections.title: Laser & Surgery
content: Focal Laser: Target MAs 50-100µm size, 0.1s duration, 'light gray' burn.
Grid Laser: Applied to areas of diffuse thickening.
Subthreshold Micropulse: Minimizes collateral RPE damage.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): Reserved for tractional DME (VMT/ERM) or refractory cases.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Endophthalmitis: Post-injection pain, redness, hypopyon.
IOP Spike: Post-steroid injection glaucoma.
Retinal Detachment: Floaters/flashes post-injection or surgery.
Ischemic Maculopathy: BCVA < 20/200 with normal CST on OCT.
Pregnancy: Caution with anti-VEGF (potential systemic absorption).

content.explanation: If vision is 20/50 or worse, Aflibercept was superior to Bevacizumab/Ranibizumab at 1 year. If 20/40 or better, all drugs performed similarly.

rows: Focal laser reduced risk of moderate vision loss by 50%.
Ranibizumab significantly improved VA vs Sham.
Observation is viable for DME with 20/25 or better vision.
Aflibercept can improve DR severity scale (DRSS) score.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for 'Disorganization of Retinal Inner Layers' (DRIL) on OCT as a prognostic marker.
DME can be 'Tractional' or 'Non-tractional'—vitrectomy only helps the former.
Hard exudates at the fovea often leave permanent scarring/subfoveal fibrosis.
NSAID drops (e.g., Nepafenac) may be an adjunct in mild, non-CI DME.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Future Trends
sections.content: Port Delivery Systems (PDS) for continuous ranibizumab release and Gene Therapy (RGX-314) aiming for 'one-and-done' treatment are currently in advanced clinical trials. Dual inhibition of Ang-2 and VEGF-A (Faricimab) represents the new standard for extending treatment intervals up to Q16 weeks.
